content: 1. If a container is leaking, place it into a larger, clearly labeled container to prevent further spillage. 2. In the event of a larger spill, contact the designated emergency phone number for assistance. 3. Specialized measures for managing and cleaning accidental spills are typically provided in the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) but are not included on the pesticide label. 4. Additional information may be accessible via a QR code on the label, if available. 5. In agricultural settings, usage instructions should align with Good Agricultural Practice (GAP) where applicable. 6. Essential instructions must always be displayed on the label, even if additional details are provided in a separate leaflet or technical literature. 7. The label should emphasize the importance of reading any attached leaflet before use, ensuring clarity for the end user. 8. Applicators, especially non-technical or occasional users, must be able to easily understand and follow the directions for use. 9. Non-essential information, such as sales messages or illustrations of the mode of action, should be omitted from the label. 10. Graphics, such as charts, graphs, symbols, or pictures, can be used to convey information in the Directions for Use section, provided they are accurate, clear, and not misleading. 11. Subheadings and bullet points should be used to organize information and make it easier to locate and understand. 12. For complex information, a tabular format may be more effective, particularly when the product is used across various crops or pests. 13. Positive statements on labels, such as references to Integrated Pest Management (IPM) or Integrated Vector Management (IVM) programs, may be included if validated by regulatory authorities. 14. Misleading statements or claims must not be used on labels. This includes false claims about product composition, safety, or efficacy, as well as superlatives like best or most effective. 15. Labels must not imply government endorsement unless explicitly authorized. 16. Bulk pesticide materials transported for reformulation, repackaging, or disposal should have appropriate labels following the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) and be accompanied by an SDS. 17. Chemically treated seeds require specific labeling, including warnings against their use for human or animal consumption and contact details for poison centers. 18. Water-soluble bags should have essential label information printed directly on the bag, such as product name, registration number, formulation type, active ingredient, and hazard symbols. 19. Insecticides for mosquito net treatment require distinct labeling, particularly for long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs). 20. Draft labels submitted to regulatory authorities must be checked for content, structure, wording, style, and quality before and after printing. 21. Labels must include all required elements, follow national regulations, and provide sufficient information to protect users and the environment. 22. The layout should be logical, with clear headings and concise, unambiguous instructions. 23. Text should predominantly be black on a white background, with a readable font size and style. 24. Printed labels must be durable, resistant to tearing, smudging, and wetting, and use inks and adhesives that withstand extreme climates and product contact. 25. Labels should warn users of pesticide hazards and classify products according to their hazards, following GHS criteria. 26. Hazard classification is based on the intrinsic properties of the pesticide product, while risk assessment evaluates the likelihood and severity of adverse effects under actual use conditions. 27. Risk assessment determines whether a pesticide can be authorized for use and identifies necessary risk mitigation measures. 28. Physical hazards of pesticides should be classified according to GHS standards, with all relevant symbols, signal words, and hazard statements displayed on the label. 29. Health hazard classifications should follow either GHS or WHO standards, depending on national regulations. 30. Labels should prioritize the classification of the pesticide formulation or end-use product rather than just the active ingredient.
